passage: "Damini didi, you know when Nanu died last winter? Everyone kept telling me, 'Darshan, he's in a better place,' and I kept thinking, how do they know? I wasn't angry exactly. Just... it cracked something open. Where did he go? Does anything I do matter if we all end? I started reading at night, anything I could find: old stories from the Upanishads, a book on black holes, even Nanu's own diary in Gujarati, which took ages. I sat in the temple some evenings and in the library some afternoons. I don't have answers. Some days that scares me. Other days it feels exciting, like I'm allowed to decide what I believe instead of just copying. Is that weird? You're the only one I can say this to."

qa.q: Whose diary did Darshan read?
qa.a: Nanu's own diary, written in Gujarati.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Darshan describe about not having answers?
qa.a: Some days the uncertainty scares Darshan, while on other days it feels exciting because Darshan gets to decide what he believes.

qa.q: What could Damini say to support Darshan?
qa.a: She could tell Darshan these questions are normal and worth having, listen without rushing to answers, and maybe share what she herself wonders about.

qa.q: How might Darshan's parents feel if they knew about the reading?
qa.a: They might be moved that Darshan is honouring Nanu, or uneasy about the questioning of what the family says, depending on how they see such doubts.

grounding: A teen tells an older didi how a loss started a search for meaning, faith and a personal philosophy.

passage: Sahil used to be the loudest one on our cricket team, always joking. This year Pankaj, that's me, noticed he'd changed. In physics, when Sir mentioned the universe was expanding, Sahil asked, "Expanding into what?" and then, "Why is there anything at all?" The class laughed. He didn't. After school he started staying back in the library with thick books from the philosophy shelf. On Sundays I saw him at the gurdwara, not just eating langar like before but serving it, quiet and focused. Once I asked him if something was wrong. He said, "No, I just want to know what I'm for." I didn't really get it. I still don't know if he's happy or worried. But he seems more awake than before, like he's listening for something.

qa.q: What did Sahil ask when the physics teacher said the universe was expanding?
qa.a: He asked what it was expanding into, and then why there is anything at all.

qa.q: What does Sahil's reply, 'I just want to know what I'm for,' suggest about his mind?
qa.a: He seems curious and searching for purpose, taking big questions about his place in the world seriously rather than as a joke.

qa.q: How could the physics teacher encourage Sahil's questions?
qa.a: He could welcome them, point him to readable books, or give time after class to talk, instead of letting the class laugh them away.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see his friend's change?
qa.a: He is puzzled and unsure whether Sahil is happy or worried, but he notices Sahil seems more awake and focused.

grounding: A friend observes a teen exploring deep questions of existence and purpose through study and spiritual practice.

passage:
First Sunday: Jasleen stood through the morning prayer at the gurdwara, thinking mostly about her maths test, the words washing past her like traffic.

The next Thursday: On a school visit to an old-age home, an old man with shaky hands held hers and asked, "Beta, what are you living for?" She laughed nervously. She had no answer. On the bus back she stared out of the window, the question stuck in her ribs.

A month later: Her notebook was titled "Things I Believe (So Far)". It had bits of Gurbani, a line from a science book about atoms made in stars, and crossed-out pages. Shankar, who called himself an atheist, argued with her at recess. "You can't prove any of it." "Maybe not," she said. "But I'm allowed to look."

qa.q: What was the title of Jasleen's notebook a month later?
qa.a: It was titled 'Things I Believe (So Far)'.

qa.q: Why did the old man's question stay with Jasleen?
qa.a: She realised she had never thought about her purpose, and not having an answer unsettled her and made her want to search.

qa.q: What small step helped Jasleen explore these questions?
qa.a: Keeping a notebook where she could collect ideas from faith and science, and cross things out as her thinking changed.

qa.q: How might Shankar see Jasleen's search?
qa.a: As an atheist he doubts her ideas can be proven, but by arguing at recess he is also taking her questions seriously.

grounding: Shows over several weeks a teen moving from routine ritual to actively exploring meaning, belief and purpose.

passage: 'You ask big questions at night, Sunaina, just like I did,' said Darshan Dada, settling his shawl. 'At sixteen I used to sleep on the roof in summer, and I would look at the stars and feel very small. What is all this for? Why am I here and not some other boy? I asked the priest at our temple, and he gave me one answer. I asked my science teacher, and she gave me another. I asked my friend the potter, who never went to school, and he said, "I don't know. But when I shape a pot, I feel joined to something." I kept all three answers for years. I still don't have just one. But I stopped being afraid of the question. It kept me company.'

qa.q: Where did young Darshan sleep in summer?
qa.a: On the roof.

qa.q: How did young Darshan feel looking at the stars?
qa.a: He felt very small and full of questions about why he existed.

qa.q: What could Sunaina take from how Darshan Dada handled these questions?
qa.a: Sunaina could ask different trusted people, keep their answers, and let the question be company rather than something scary.

qa.q: How does the potter's answer differ from the other two?
qa.a: It comes from feeling and daily work rather than teaching or scripture, showing meaning can be found in doing.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring questions of existence by gathering spiritual, scientific and personal answers.

passage: Yamini had planned the sunrise walk with Ritu for weeks, but at five Ritu texted that she had a fever and couldn't come. Yamini went up the hill behind the town alone. Fog swallowed the view; there would be no sunrise. She sat on the wet bench anyway, annoyed, hood up. Lately every question in her head ended the same way: what is the point of any of it, marks, college, even being kind? Her family prayed every evening; her best friend believed in nothing she could name. Yamini didn't know where she stood. In the fog she could hear a temple bell below, a dog, someone's pressure cooker. For one strange second she felt part of all of it. She typed to Ritu: 'No sunrise. But something. Tell you later.'

qa.q: Why couldn't Ritu come on the walk?
qa.a: She had a fever.

qa.q: What did Yamini feel for 'one strange second' in the fog?
qa.a: She felt connected to everything around her, a sense of belonging her questions hadn't given her.

qa.q: What might help Yamini keep exploring these questions?
qa.a: Talking them over with Ritu, her family or a teacher she trusts, and reading different views, without rushing to settle on one.

qa.q: How might Ritu react to the message 'No sunrise. But something'?
qa.a: She would probably be curious and a bit sorry she missed it, and keen to hear what Yamini meant.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager wrestling with questions of purpose and glimpsing a feeling of universal connection on a foggy morning.
